title: Moments of mind
hookLine: consciousness as a stream of tiny moments, each arising and passing
last: THREE REALITIES PASS; NIBBANA ALONE IS UNMADE.

lines: NO RUNNING ON ANY ONE PAGE.
cards: A flip book is a small stack of paper with a drawing in the corner of every page. Each drawing is still: a stick figure with one leg forward, then the leg a little further, then further.
Riffle the stack with your thumb, and the figure runs. It looks like one smooth motion, but there's no running on any single page. The running happens in the flipping.
Today the first drawer opens, and the Abhidhamma says the mind is a little like that flip book.

teach.h: ONE MOMENT OF KNOWING AT A TIME.
teach.b: Today's word is citta, usually put into English as mind, or consciousness: the knowing of something. First, the Abhidhamma's claim. Mind isn't one steady light left on all day.
It's a stream of tiny moments of knowing, each arising, staying for an instant, and passing away, followed by the next. The commentaries give each moment three phases: arising, standing, dissolving.
Second, the seed of this in the suttas.
In the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha pictures a monkey moving through a forest: it grabs a branch, lets it go, grabs another.
In paraphrase, he says what we call mind is like that: by day and by night, it arises as one thing and ceases as another.

And in the Anguttara Nikaya, he says he can't point to anything that changes as quickly as the mind. Third, why it matters. If mind is one steady thing, a bad mood can seem like a fact about who someone is.

teach.h: THE NEXT PAGE ISN'T DRAWN YET.
teach.b: If mind is moments, the bad mood is a run of pages in the flip book, and the next page isn't drawn yet.

The Dhammapada opens, in Max Müller's translation, with a line some readers hear alongside this: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts."
Fourth, the quiet surprise. Watched closely, the stream doesn't need a watcher behind it. The knowing of an itch is one moment; the knowing that you noticed it is the next.
There's riffling, and figures running, and no one sitting inside the book.

how: In Theravada insight meditation, practitioners watch thoughts, sounds and sensations arise and pass, and teachers often explain what they see using the Abhidhamma's account of mind as a stream of moments.

o: one long thought that lasts all day
the mind as a stream of brief moments of knowing
the heart, the seat of feeling apart from thought

games.q: moment by moment: tap the pairs.
p: grabs a branch, lets go, grabs another
the running happens in the flipping

s: the Abhidhamma pictures mind as one steady light left on all day
it pictures a stream of tiny moments of knowing, one at a time, each arising and passing.
in the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha says nothing changes as quickly as the mind
he says he can't point to anything that changes so quickly.
the Dhammapada opens by saying we are made up of our thoughts
in Max Müller's words: "it is made up of our thoughts."

games.q: a monkey is moving through the forest. it grabs a branch. what does it do next, in the Buddha's picture of the mind?
o: holds that branch and never lets go
lets it go and grabs another
climbs down and sits still forever
games.why: it lets go and grabs another, and another: what we call mind, the Buddha says, arises as one thing and ceases as another, by day and by night.

practice: If you'd like, watch the mind the way you'd watch a road from a window, not chasing thoughts and not pushing them away: a thought appears and goes, then a sound, a memory, a plan for dinner.
If you get carried off on one, that's the monkey grabbing a branch; notice that too, and come back to watching. You're not trying to stop the flicker, only to see that it flickers.

wordCard.voice: Citta. Consciousness, the knowing of something, which the Abhidhamma sees as a stream of tiny moments, each arising and passing. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: mind, consciousness, the knowing of something.

carryVoice: Your line: moment by moment. A mood is a run of pages, not the whole book. Same time tomorrow.
